description: We are forming an international team to explore how AI and NASA’s microgravity combustion research can support safer human space exploration. For the “Flame in Freefall” challenge, we aim to create an interactive dashboard that turns complex experimental findings into clear, accessible, and evidence-based fire safety insights. Our focus is on scientific accuracy, useful visualizations, and explanations linked to their original sources.
summary:
Flame Atlas is an interactive research dashboard developed by Team Aero-Engineer to make NASA’s microgravity combustion research easier to explore and interpret. The prototype organizes ten evidence records from six NASA sources, including research articles, a technical report abstract, and Physical Sciences Informatics investigation descriptions.

Users can search with questions, filter findings by experiment, fuel type or research topic, compare records, and download results. AI-assisted summaries present findings alongside their sources, research implications and limitations. A transparent text-retrieval model ranks relevant records and produces a source-linked reading brief.

The project addresses the Flame in Freefall challenge by bringing scattered combustion evidence into an accessible interface. It helps researchers and students investigate questions about flame detection, suppression, atmospheric conditions and experimental scale—topics relevant to future spacecraft fire-safety research. Flame Atlas is a working evidence-exploration prototype, not a validated fire-prediction system; it preserves this distinction by clearly separating published findings from interpretations.
details:
Flame Atlas is an interactive research dashboard that helps users explore NASA’s microgravity combustion research. Developed by Team Aero-Engineer, it addresses the difficulty of finding and comparing findings across experiments involving different fuels, atmospheric conditions and experimental scales.

What it does

The prototype organizes ten qualitative evidence records from six NASA sources, covering research associated with BASS, BASS-II, SoFIE-GEL, FLEX, CFI-G and Saffire. Each record includes a finding, its source, a research implication and an explicit limitation.

Users can:

  • Search the evidence using questions or keywords.
  • Filter results by research topic, fuel type or experiment.
  • Read a brief assembled from the highest-ranked findings.
  • Compare up to three records side by side.
  • Open the original NASA sources.
  • Download filtered results as JSON, including source links and search context.

How it works

Flame Atlas uses a local text-retrieval model based on Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). This method assigns weights to words according to their frequency within a record and across the evidence collection. Cosine similarity then ranks records according to their textual relevance to the user’s query.

The interface displays matched words and relevance scores, making the ranking understandable. These scores represent text similarity, not scientific confidence or fire risk. When a query has no matching evidence, the dashboard explicitly reports that gap. Reading briefs reuse source-linked summaries rather than generating new scientific claims.

For example, searching “cool flame detection” retrieves records about FLEX and CFI-G. Users can compare their liquid- and gaseous-fuel contexts, inspect the reported findings and follow the NASA source links.

Benefits and intended impact

The project aims to make combustion research more accessible to students and researchers while preserving the context needed to interpret it responsibly. It supports preliminary investigation of questions about flame detection, suppression, material behavior, atmospheric conditions and experimental scale.

Its intended contribution to future spacecraft fire-safety research is better evidence navigation. It does not replace expert assessment, experimental testing or engineering validation. No measured improvement in safety or research efficiency is claimed.

Tools and development

The application uses HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, with evidence stored in JavaScript and JSON files. It runs in a standard web browser without installation, specialized hardware or an API key. The complete project can be downloaded, extracted and opened locally through index.html.

ChatGPT assisted with implementation, interface design, source paraphrasing and documentation. The running application uses deterministic text retrieval, not a live generative AI service.

Creative approach

Flame Atlas combines evidence discovery with an explicit distinction between published findings, project interpretations and applicability limits. Instead of presenting an isolated answer, it gives users a traceable reading brief and a comparison workflow. Its emphasis is on helping users understand why a result is relevant and what it cannot establish.

Factors considered and limitations

Development prioritized source traceability, understandable ranking, accessibility and ease of sharing. The evidence collection uses published summaries, a technical report abstract and investigation metadata; it does not contain raw experimental time series. PSI metadata was obtained from indexed investigation descriptions.

The small corpus and lexical retrieval method can miss relevant concepts or synonyms. The prototype has no trained combustion predictor, CFD simulation or quantitative fire-risk model. Microgravity findings also cannot automatically establish behavior under lunar or Martian surface gravity.

Future development would include run-level PSI data ingestion, consistent units and experimental-condition fields, combustion-specialist review, and retrieval evaluation against expert-labeled questions.
